CONTEXT (from f.202). Gauss is evaluating his refraction integral for an atmosphere in which pressure and density follow e = E(1-s/g) and c = C(1-s/g)^lambda, with s = 1-R/r. This means temperature decreases linearly with height. The refraction is R'' = -∫ mu dx/(2(1-mu x)) · sinJ / sqrt(b - sin^2 J). Here b = (1-mu x)/(1-s)^2 and s = g[1-(1-x)^(1/lambda)], so x = 1-c/C.

[Mine] He substitutes x = y^2 (dx = 2y dy). This removes the 1/sqrt(x) singularity at the lower limit, which matters near the horizon. The integrand becomes mu y dy/(1-mu y^2) · sinJ/sqrt(b - sin^2J).

[Mine] Put 1/b = 1-BB. Then sin^2J/b = sin^2J(1-BB), so b - sin^2J = b cos^2J(1+BB tan^2J). Each quadrature term is therefore
 A tanJ / sqrt(1+BB tan^2J), with
 a = rho''·k mu y/(1-mu y^2),
 A = a sqrt(1-BB),
 BB = (2s - s^2 - mu y^2)/(1-mu y^2),
 s = g[1-(1-y^2)^(1/lambda)].
This is exactly the scheme of f.202.

The quadrature is 7-point Gauss-Legendre on [0,1] ('meine Quadraturcoefficienten' k):
- y = 0.0254460, 0.1292344, 0.2970774, 0.5, 0.7029226, 0.8707656, 0.9745540.
- log y = 8.4056202, 9.1113781, 9.4728696, 9.6989700, 9.8469075, 9.9399013, 9.9888059.
- k = 0.0647425, 0.1398527, 0.1909150, 0.2089796 (symmetric).
- log k = 8.8111894, 9.1456708, 9.2808401, 9.3201039.

Constants:
- log mu = 6.74708, so mu = 5.585e-4 (about 2(n-1)).
- log lambda = 0.72853, so lambda = 5.352.
- log g = 7.90811, so g = 0.0080915. With g = (lambda+1)l/R this gives l/R ≈ 0.001274. T reaches zero at h = gR ≈ 51 km, i.e. a lapse rate of about 5.3 K/km.
- The additive constant should be log(mu·206265'') = 6.74708 + 5.31443 = 2.06151. Gauss first used 2.08151, later corrected (see below).

Computation for each node y (all in 7-place logs):
(i) log(k y mu rho) = log y + log k + 2.08151.
(ii) log(1-mu y^2).
(iii) log a = (i) - (ii).
(iv) log(1-y^2). Then log|log(1-y^2)| - log lambda gives |log (1-y^2)^(1/lambda)|. Antilog gives (1-y^2)^(1/lambda), hence w = 1-(1-y^2)^(1/lambda) and s = g w.
(v) Natural numbers: 2gw - g^2w^2 - mu y^2, then divide by (1-mu y^2) to get BB.
(vi) log B = ½ log BB; log sqrt(1-BB); log A = log a + log sqrt(1-BB).

Then log w = 7.4972, log s = 5.4053, giving BB and log B = 7.80917. As a check he uses f.202's series BB ≈ 0.002465624 yy(1+yy/2): 7.39193 + 8.22276 + 0.00361 = 5.61830 (direct value ≈ 5.6183).

results.what: Numerical evaluation of the astronomical refraction integral by 7-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature on [0,1], after the substitution x = y^2 that removes the endpoint square-root singularity
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Methodus nova integralium valores per approximationem inveniendi, 1814/1816)

results.what: Refraction model with polytropic atmosphere: pressure ∝ (1-s/g), density ∝ (1-s/g)^lambda, i.e. temperature linearly decreasing with height (lambda ≈ 5.35, implied lapse ≈ 5.3 K/km)
results.usually_credited_to: Ivory (1823/1838); related forms by Laplace and Bessel; Gauss's own treatment largely unpublished

results.what: Recasting of each quadrature term as A tanJ/sqrt(1+B^2 tan^2 J), with B^2 = (2s-s^2-mu y^2)/(1-mu y^2), so a single table of (A,B) serves all zenith distances
results.modern_name: tabulated quadrature form of refraction R(J) = Σ A_i tanJ / sqrt(1+B_i^2 tan^2 J)

results.what: Numerical results: refraction constant ΣA = 57.56", horizontal refraction 34'31.8", refraction at 89° = 24'13.8"
results.usually_credited_to: standard tables of Bradley, Bessel (Fundamenta 1818, Tabulae Regiomontanae 1830)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss quadrature is his own, and his interest in refraction is known. Still, a fully worked application of his 7-point formula to the refraction integral of a constant-lapse-rate atmosphere is a notable unpublished detail. This includes the singularity-removing substitution, a horizontal refraction of 34'31", and a lapse rate of about 5 K/km, predating Ivory's 1823 polytropic theory. It is not a new theorem, so the score stays modest.
